title: Göbekli Tepe and the First Monuments

cards.h: The temple that arrived before the farm
cards.b:
Imagine finding a giant stone circle, older than Stonehenge by about 6,000 years, built by people who had not yet invented pottery or the wheel.

In 1994, a German archaeologist, Klaus Schmidt, walked up a bare hill in south-east Turkey and noticed something.

Göbekli Tepe (Turkish for 'Potbelly Hill') is near Şanlıurfa. Its tall T-shaped limestone pillars, some about 5 metres high and weighing many tonnes, stand in circles. They date to about 9500-8000 BCE.

Many pillars are carved with foxes, boars, snakes, vultures and scorpions. Some pillars look like stylised people, with arms and hands carved on the sides.

cards.h: Which came first: the temple or the farm?
cards.b:
Schmidt suggested that a gathering place for ritual might have pushed people to settle and farm, because feeding crowds needed food. 'First the temple, then the city', he said.

This flips the usual story. Some scholars agree. Others point out that people also lived and worked nearby, so it may not have been only a temple.
After about 1,500 years, the site was filled in deliberately. Nobody knows why. Excavation has uncovered only a small part of the site so far, so we may still be missing the story.

These builders had no metal tools and no wheels or beasts of burden. They cut pillars with flint tools from a nearby quarry and moved them by rope and muscle.

That needed hundreds of people working together. Who organised them? We do not know. There are no kings or written laws from this time to tell us.

Later, humans built bigger things. Stonehenge's big stones went up around 2500 BCE. The Megalithic temples of Malta are about 3600-3200 BCE. In Egypt, the first pyramid, Djoser's, was built around 2670 BCE.

Göbekli Tepe is older than all of these, by thousands of years.

cards.h: Was it built by aliens or a lost civilisation?
cards.b: Myth: some popular shows claim Göbekli Tepe proves a 'lost advanced civilisation'.Fact: there is no evidence for this. The tools, bones and carvings are consistent with hunter-gatherer communities. The truly amazing thing is that ordinary people did it. Archaeologists dislike the 'lost civilisation' idea, and it can dismiss the skill of ancient people.

India's own monument builders

Göbekli Tepe's pillars rose around 9500 BCE, before farming. India's stone builders came much later, but they were just as determined. At Burzahom in Kashmir, about 3000 BCE, people lived in pits and raised standing stones, and buried dogs with their owners.

Then came the megaliths. From about 1000 BCE, communities in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Kerala laid out stone circles and chambers for the dead. Hire Benkal in Karnataka has hundreds of them.

In Meghalaya the Khasi still raise menhirs today, so the old habit has never quite stopped.

Five things to remember

  1. Göbekli Tepe dates to about 9500-8000 BCE.
  2. It was built before farming was established.
  3. Pillars carry animal carvings.
  4. Nobody knows why it was buried.
  5. The 'lost civilisation' claim has no evidence.

Think about it

  • What does it say about people that they organised big projects before farms?
  • Why does it matter that only a small part has been dug?
